b: It’s five answers to five questions. Here we go…
1. Should I tell coworkers I’m leaving because of them?

I’ve spent the last year in a work environment where my coworkers have ranged from unfriendly to hostile, but only to me. There are only five of us and I’ve been the odd person out since I joined. It’s ranged from clique-ish behavior to micromanaging (even from a coworker with less experience than me!) to condescending discussions to childish bullying. We are all in the field of mental health, so to be treated this way is especially upsetting. For reasons I can’t detail here without potentially doxing myself, we are not in a position where the manager can fire anyone.

I’ve talked with my manager about this several times over the last year, and she has made some unsuccessful attempts to address it with the others. She understands my reason for leaving, and we will continue working together with me in more of a contractor capacity. That said, I’d like to let the group know I’m leaving and WHY. Not to be vindictive, but because I think they need to know their behavior is pushing people out. Any recommendations for how I could word this?

I don’t think you should. It’s useful for your manager know, and it sounds like she does. A good manager would address the culture (and, frankly, management) issues that allowed this to happen but it doesn’t sound like she’s equipped to do that, for whatever reason. There’s very little to be gained by you explaining your reason for leaving to the others; you don’t owe them that, and it risks backfiring or at least not being received the way you hope. They might just minimize your experience or decide you’re over-sensitive. And to be clear, it’s not that they don’t need to hear some feedback — they do! — but you’re not the person who can most effectively deliver it, particularly as you’re leaving … and I’m not convinced they’ll feel remorse or understand why their behavior was unacceptable, especially since your manager has already been unsuccessful in talking with them about it.

I fully understand feeling like people should know their behavior has consequences. But it isn’t your responsibility to educate them or improve their team. You’ve already spent a year dealing with it; you’re allowed to just leave without doing more emotional labor for them.

That said, you’re certainly allowed to tell them the truth about your experience if you want to. In theory, you could say something brief like, “Since joining our team, I’ve often felt excluded and singled out, and I’ve had many interactions that have felt condescending and unkind, and that’s played a role in my decision to leave.” But before doing that, I’d ask yourself how you’ll feel if no one acknowledges it at all and nothing changes. If you’d still be glad you said it, maybe that’s an argument for it! But if that would bother you, don’t give them more power over your mental peace; just leave and be done with them.
2. I was blindsided by a vandalism investigation

I was called into the department head’s office the other day and blindsided with an HR video call investigation. I was told I was being recorded and the HR lady was going to be investigating an incident and taking notes. I had no idea of anything happening or anything I had done wrong.

It turned out that at some point during a previous shift, someone attempted to vandalize one of the supervisor’s offices. Everyone has access to these areas, with and without a key depending if it’s locked or not. I was told that during the time they were reviewing, I was the only person seen entering the area and leaving. I absolutely did nothing but get a bag of chips when in there (there’s a common snack area). They asked all sorts of questions.

I felt attacked, blindsided, and ultimately targeted by all of this. I have been with the company for a long, long time and have never done or would do anything to anyone or their property. The meeting concluded with no back-up from my boss whatsoever.
Is there something I should do to protect myself? I did nothing wrong at all and am worried!

First, being questioned about this doesn’t mean that HR has decided you did anything wrong. If video footage showed you entering and leaving an area where an incident occurred, it makes sense that they wanted to talk to you; they need to establish who had access and what they observed.

It’s a good idea to follow up with HR in writing, and cc’ your manager. Send a calm, professional message saying something like, “I want to follow up on our meeting and reiterate that I had no involvement in any vandalism or damage to company property. My reason for entering the area during the shift in question was to obtain a bag of chips from the snack area. I did not damage, alter, or otherwise interfere with anyone’s property. Given the seriousness of the situation and my long employment with the company, I hope it’s clear that I did not play a role in this, and I will of course cooperate fully and answer any additional questions as accurately as possible.”

You could also talk with your boss privately and say something like, “I was really taken aback by that meeting. I have a long track record here of responsible behavior and no history of anything like that, and I don’t want that jeopardized. Can you clarify whether there are any concerns about my standing with the company at this point?”
3. I got an infection from a work vaccine clinic and have to use PTO for it

A few weeks ago, my workplace held a vaccine clinic as part of our benefits. I love vaccines and I think they’re good, and I’m still a fan despite my bad reaction. I got an infection from my injection — the doctor said that the nurse had probably missed the disinfected injection site. It got bad enough I had to go to the emergency room and get medicated. I’ve had to take several days off — all our time off is in the same bracket. It’s not really my company’s fault, or really anyone’s, but I’ve gotten really sick and had to eat into my limited PTO budget. Is there anything I can do or ask for?

It’s possible (but not definite) that this could be covered under workers’ comp because it was a workplace clinic and thus may be considered a work-related injury. Tell HR you developed an infection at the injection site that became serious enough to require emergency room treatment and medication, and that it took several days of PTO to recover. Ask whether it should be reported through the company’s workers’ comp insurance, and also ask whether they would consider restoring those days to your PTO balance.
Outside of workers’ comp laws, your company probably doesn’t have any legal obligation to restore the PTO, but they might be willing to do it as a good-will gesture.
4. Should I agree to a sale contingent on my continued employment?

I’m a minority owner of a small business looking to sell. A distant colleague of mine in another state, with no current ties to the company, wants to buy the entire business, contingent on my staying on as GM. I’ve been willing to do that.

I found out this week though, that the ownership group (including me) would carry the financing. I don’t love carrying a note at all, but especially not for my employer. Essentially, I’d be a lender and a subordinate. I’m a great GM. I’m a good employee. I can’t imagine taking orders from someone who owes me tens of thousands of dollars, though. I wish my personality wasn’t that flawed, but I know myself and can admit it.

Should I even entertain this? My business attorney says the new owners should pay my portion out, or I shouldn’t work there. But if I say I’m not staying, it could tank the sale for everyone and I feel guilty.
Your attorney’s suggestion is the right one. If they want you to do this, they should buy you out first so you don’t have conflicting roles.
Keep in mind that you aren’t saying “I’m not staying” but rather, “Here’s what I’d need to make this work” … and then it’s up to them if they want to do that or not.
5. My title changed but my job is the same

My department has recently gone through a review process, and one of the outcomes was that many people’s job titles have been changed. So if my title was previously, for example, “teapot officer,” let’s say it’s now “teapot specialist.” Nothing else about my role has substantially changed.
How do I handle this on my resume going forward? I don’t want to make it look like I’m misleading people into thinking I got a new position when I didn’t.
You can list it like this:

Teapot Emporium, January 2021 – present
Teapot Specialist, September 2026 – present
Teapot Officer, January 2021 – August 2026
It’s not misleading anyone into thinking it’s a whole new job; it’s a factually accurate account of your titles there, and you’re still grouping what you did in that role under one overall heading.
